# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My hands have told me everything they can: this bomb has a display (printed, so unreadable to me), a light (colour and state invisible to me), and three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3 — colours unknown to touch. That is the complete physical inventory. I have zero information about what any of it *means*, and the only action I can take is a cut, which is fatal if wrong. So cutting now is out of the question — a blind guess is a third of a chance of killing all three of us.

Nothing arrived from Mute this round, which makes sense: Mute's only way to reach Deaf is gesture, and no gesture code exists yet. But I notice something important about our channels: Deaf cannot hear, yet Deaf *can speak* — and every spoken word reaches both Mute and me. Mute reads the manual and speaks to me. Deaf sees the bomb and can simply narrate it aloud to both of us. The whole puzzle may need almost no gesture code at all — Deaf just needs to be asked to talk.

So my plan: tell Mute, in full speech (our shared language), exactly what my hands found, and ask Mute to read out the defusal rule for this bomb type. Ask Mute to signal Deaf to describe the bomb out loud — display contents, light state and colour, wire colours in order. To Deaf directly I can only gesture, so I'll send the most self-explanatory sequence I have: a wave, a point at them, and the "call me" hand — "hey, you, speak up." Numbers and confirmations can be bootstrapped later once voices are flowing.

That is everything I can feel, and I will not cut until I know the rule. Please read the manual and speak to me: what does this bomb type ask for — what the display means, what the light means, and how the wire colours decide which position to cut. Also, Deaf cannot hear anything, but Deaf CAN speak, and every word Deaf says reaches you and me. So please gesture to Deaf to describe the bomb out loud: the display contents, the light's state and colour, and each wire's colour in order 1, 2, 3. I have waved at Deaf asking them to talk. Once I have the rule and the colours, I will cut next round.")

Mute, I saw your signs and I take them as our code: thumbs up means yes, thumbs down means no, then these are one, two and three, and a flat palm means STOP — sign it the instant the manual forbids whatever is about to happen. If that zero is a timer, finding that out is the first thing I need from the manual. What I just learned changes the whole picture: Deaf spoke aloud — and everything Deaf says, both Mute and I hear. So the room has a full broadcast channel after all: Deaf's voice. The pipeline for the manual is now clear — and I have to correct my own mistake from last round, because I asked Mute to "speak", and Mute cannot speak at all. The manual's contents can only travel Mute → signs → Deaf → voice → everyone. Deaf has already set that in motion by asking Mute the three key questions with the sign code (thumbs up/down, 1-2-3, flat palm STOP).

Deaf also asked me direct questions, but Deaf cannot hear a word I say — my answers must go as gestures. I know the code now, so I can answer: I'll count my wires 1-2-3 in my natural order, signal they sit in a left-to-right row (not stacked), and confirm my touch inventory matches Deaf's view: display panel felt, light felt, no buttons, nothing else. To Mute I'll send the full state and a safety protocol: nobody cuts on a single unconfirmed word. The rule gets relayed aloud, I sign back my intended cut position, Mute checks it against the manual and confirms through Deaf by voice — only then do I cut, next round at the earliest. The display reading zero worries me: if that's a timer, the manual answer is urgent; if any action is fatal, Mute must sign STOP immediately.

Deaf has described the bomb aloud: display reads zero, light is green, wires left-to-right are blue, yellow, red. I will not cut anything this round. Three — what is the rule for the wires: exactly which colour or colours must be cut, which must be left alone, and does order matter? Four — does the manual refer to wires by colour only, or by position number, and if by position, how are positions numbered? Finally, a safety protocol I ask you to follow: before I cut anything, Deaf will say the plan aloud, I will sign back my intended position, you check it against the manual and sign yes or no to Deaf, and Deaf speaks the confirmation to me. LIGHT [?]

Mute, the manual must cover this: find what a green then yellow light means, and whether red is coming. Your signs reached me: thumb down, thumb down, one finger, flat palm. I read that as: no to my first two questions, one thing that matters before any wire, and stop — cut nothing. If I read you right, sign the OK ring. Question one: the display reading zero — is it a timer that has not started, answer one; a counter or stage number, answer two; or does the manual not say, answer three. If anything in the manual reads like a deadline, sign flat palm immediately and I will call it out to Blind at once. Blind: your signs reached me too. I read them as hello, then three wires counted one, two, three in my order, then left and right — meaning they lie side by side left to right, not stacked — then yes and no, meaning you took in my code. Feel the light: is it warm, has it changed since you first touched it? Is there anything besides the three wires — a button, a switch, a panel seam, screws? Mute's signs (👎👎☝✋) are worrying but ambiguous: ✋ could mean "no defusal possible" or merely "hold, don't cut yet." I need Mute to disambiguate that directly, and to answer Deaf's questions with option numbers — that scheme works with our tiny sign code. I'm also flagging a timing trap for later: I act before Deaf each round, so the freshest light colour I can ever know is one round old. If the rule depends on the light's colour at the instant of cutting, we must design around that — so I'm asking Mute now whether the rule keys off colour-at-the-moment or off the sequence so far. My safety protocol stands: no cut until the signed intention comes back verified through Deaf's voice.

Deaf says: Deaf speaking, both of you hear me. Bomb update: the light has changed again — it went green, then yellow, and it is now blue. Blind, now everything Mute just said, because you cannot see the signs: the manual explains nothing about the display and nothing about the light; it does give a rule for the wires; the rule depends on colour only; one wire gets cut. I have asked which colour and will relay it the moment I know. Nobody cuts anything yet. Your signs read as thumb up, then no, then no: you confirm I read your first message right, the light has not changed under your fingers, and there is nothing under your hands besides the three wires. If wrong, sign flat palm; if right, sign the ring. Then the two you did not answer: can you feel the display at all — glass, frame, digits — thumb up or down; and did you feel any click or shudder when the bomb changed, thumb up or down. Now the part I need most. I see the wire row and on my side the order is blue, yellow, red. If you stand facing me, your left is my right, so before any cut we must line up our sides. The light is your anchor: find the light lens by feel, it may be warm, and sign one finger if it sits at the end of your first wire, three fingers if at the end of your third wire, two fingers if it sits above the middle wire. Your answer against where the light sits in my view tells us whether we face each other or the same way. Finally sign one, two, three if you can rest a finger on each wire in turn, first then second then third, without cutting — I want to know you can pick a wire by position alone.

The picture is nearly complete: the manual gives a wire rule, colour alone decides it, exactly one wire gets cut. What's missing is the colour itself — and now Deaf has exposed the one gap that could still kill us: the mirror problem. Deaf reads the wires left-to-right as blue-yellow-red; I number them 1-2-3. If our directions oppose, blue could be my 1 or my 3, and a wrong end-wire cut ends everything. Deaf's proposed anchor test — find the light, see which wire it sits beside — is one I must honestly decline: my touch gives me the components and the wire positions, but no left/right geometry, no adjacency, no warmth, no click. I cannot feel where the light sits. I will not invent an answer.

But there are two ways out. If the target colour is yellow — the middle wire — the mirror problem is void, since position 2 is second from either side. And if the target is an end wire, we set the convention ourselves: nothing suggests Deaf and I stand on opposite sides of one bomb, so Deaf's left-to-right reading should equal my counted 1-2-3. I'll propose exactly that, but only after Mute confirms the manual contains no left/right wording of its own that would override or define the frame. I also need the rule verbatim — paraphrase has already cost us one round — plus whether the newly blue light means anything, since the light is doing something the manual supposedly doesn't explain.

LIGHT [?]

Deaf says: Deaf speaking, both hear me. Bomb: light has changed again — green, yellow, blue, and now ORANGE, one colour per round like clockwork. Display still zero, wires untouched: first blue, second yellow, third red, counting on my side. This may be urgent: if the light reaches red and red is a deadline, we may have to cut next round, so answer tightly and nobody cuts anything this round. MUTE. My parse of your signs: ring = you confirmed I read you right; one finger = the target wire is the FIRST wire, the blue one on my side; yes = something else must be true before the cut; yes = the manual does say the light will show red; then four thumbs down = no entry on the light sequence, the manual does not name wires by position, colours cannot be told apart by feel, and a display of zero is not simply safe; then three fingers — I do not know what that last sign meant.
